summary: An evidence-based "learn how to learn" course done on your own Kerala PSC material. Measure your memory, reading, focus and digit span in week 0 and again at the end; build a 100-card AnkiDroid deck, a memory palace, five Feynman recordings, a PYQ analysis and error log, a 12-week PSC study plan and a 30-day learning sprint. sections.title: Start here: how this course works
sections.summary: What you will build and measure, how long it takes, how evidence is rated, where each topic is taught, the PSC fast path and the assumptions behind the course.
sections.content:
## What this course is

A free, practical "learn how to learn" course that you do on your own study material. Every lesson teaches one evidence-based method, says honestly how strong the research behind it is, and ends with an action task on your real Kerala PSC subjects: GK, current affairs, the Constitution, Kerala, maths and reasoning, English and Malayalam. Lesson by lesson, the tasks build one **personal learning system** that you keep using for PSC and for everything you learn after it: AI skills, business, languages.

It is written for a PSC aspirant near Kuttiady in Kozhikode district with an Android phone, an old laptop and ₹0 to spend. It works for anyone preparing for a competitive exam.

## By the end you will have

- **Measured results:** four baseline tests in week 0 (list recall after 10 minutes and 24 hours, reading speed with comprehension, focus duration, digit span), repeated with fresh versions in week 28
- **An AnkiDroid deck** of 100 or more well-made cards on one PSC topic, reviewed every day for 30 days, and a daily review habit
- **A memory palace** that holds a real PSC topic
- **Five recorded Feynman explanations** of PSC topics, each improved after listening back
- **A previous-year question analysis and an error log** for your target exam
- **A complete 12-week PSC study and revision plan**
- **A lesson you taught** to a family member or study partner
- **A 30-day learning sprint** with before and after tests and a reflection report
- **The Learning Workbook and Learning Folder** that hold the whole system: planner, revision schedule, card checklist, error log, Feynman template and weekly review

## How long it takes

| Pace | Calendar time | Hours a week | Total work |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Part-time (the default) | Week 0, then 28 weeks: about 6.5 months | About 6 (5 to 7) | About 160 hours |
| Full-time | About 11 weeks | About 15 | About 160 hours |

Pick your pace and start date on the course page; the app then shows your week and what is due. Two things take real days at any pace: the 30-day AnkiDroid review and the 30-day capstone sprint. Much of the action-task time is also PSC study, because you do it on your own syllabus.

## Honest expectations

- **Your list recall will improve the most,** because techniques such as chunking and the memory palace work quickly. The list test shows it.
- **Your digit span will change little.** Working memory capacity is fairly stable. A large review of "brain training" found gains on trained tasks but no convincing improvement in reading, arithmetic or intelligence ([Melby-Lervåg and others, 2016](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:daa9a729-f17b-4e45-97c0-cff5075ea404)). A gain of one digit usually comes from a better strategy, such as chunking.
- **Reading speed will rise a little; comprehension can rise more.** No method lets you read several times faster with full understanding ([APS, 2016](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/releases/speed-reading-promises-are-too-good-to-be-true-scientists-find.html)). The test reports your **effective reading rate**: speed multiplied by comprehension.
- **Focus depends mostly on habits and your phone.** It usually improves a lot once the phone is out of reach.
- **What matters most is your exam score.** Retrieval practice and spaced practice have the strongest evidence of any study methods ([Dunlosky, 2013](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky)). The capstone measures the change on a real PSC subject.
- **Some weeks will go badly.** The weekly review is where you notice and adjust, without guilt.

## How strong is the evidence?

Every lesson has a short evidence table. The ratings mean:

**Strong:** many studies, in labs and real classrooms, agree. **Moderate:** good studies, but fewer, narrower or with mixed results. **Limited:** small or indirect studies; use it as a practical tool and judge it by your own results. **No good evidence:** tested and not supported.

When research is thin, the lesson says so. Some popular methods in this course (the Feynman technique, Pomodoro, SQ3R, mind maps) have little direct research. They are included because they put well-supported principles into practice, and you will test them on your own results.

## How each lesson works

1. **ID, title, outcome and time** at the top, such as LRN-M01-L01
2. **Core lesson:** the idea, explained simply
3. **Local example:** the idea used by PSC aspirants in Kozhikode district
4. **How strong is the evidence?** an honest rating
5. **Free resources:** exactly what to study, how long it takes, and when the link was checked
6. **Action task:** real work on your PSC material, and the **proof to record**
7. **Template:** copy-ready tools for your Learning Workbook or notebook
8. **Common mistakes** and how to avoid them
9. **Quiz:** 3 to 5 questions, with answers at the very bottom
10. **Progress checklist:** the ticks under **Your tasks**

Each module starts with an overview page: outcomes, time, the tools it adds, the module project, a self-assessment rubric, a "short on time?" version and revision flashcards.

## Where each topic is taught

The modules are ordered so your system starts working early: the six strategies and AnkiDroid in the first month, focus, habits and self-testing in the second, and exam mastery by week 15, so your 12-week PSC plan runs during the rest of the course.

## PSC exam soon? Take the fast path

- **Exam within 8 weeks:** do Week 0, then Module 3 (the six strategies), Module 4 (AnkiDroid), LRN-M05-L03 (phone), Module 12 (exam mastery) and LRN-M19-L01 (sleep). Return to the rest after the exam.
- **Exam within 12 to 16 weeks:** follow the normal order to the end of Module 4, then do Module 12 and start your 12-week plan. Continue with Modules 5 onwards alongside the plan.
- **No exam date yet:** follow the normal order.

On the course page, mark the lessons you skip as done later, or move your start date; your ticks are kept either way.

## Key assumptions

These decisions were made when the course was written. Change them if your situation is different.

1. **Pace:** part-time, about 6 hours a week (5 to 7) for 28 weeks after week 0. The full-time pace does the same work in about 11 weeks at about 15 hours a week.
2. **Your PSC study continues.** The course changes **how** you study, not **what**. Action tasks use your syllabus, books and question papers, so they count as PSC study too.
3. **Target exam:** you choose one Kerala PSC exam (for example LDC, LGS, a Degree Level or Plus Two Level preliminary, or a department test) and download its syllabus in week 0. Examples use topics common to most general exams.
4. **Devices:** the Android phone does nearly everything (AnkiDroid, Google Sheets, voice recorder, timer). The laptop helps with long typing and PDFs, and can run Anki for computers if it has Windows 10 or later or a recent Linux.
5. **Money:** ₹0. Every tool and resource is free. No paid coaching, apps or AI plans are needed.
6. **Language:** simple English. Key terms have Malayalam meanings in the glossary.
7. **Facts in examples** (articles of the Constitution, rivers, awards) were checked on 2026-11-03. PSC answer keys follow official textbooks, so check your own book when they differ.
8. **Health:** the brain-health module gives general guidance, not medical advice. See a doctor for sleep, mood or health problems.
9. **Privacy:** your recordings, notes and scores stay in your own Learning Folder. Your progress in this app is saved on your phone only.

## The running examples (all made up)

- **Anu**, 27, from Kakkattil: preparing for LDC and the Degree Level preliminary while tutoring students in the evenings (you may know her from the Personal Finance course)
- **Sreeja**, 34, from Nadapuram: a homemaker with two children, studying for LGS in two 45-minute slots a day
- **Ashiq**, 22, from Kuttiady: a new BCom graduate, good at maths, fighting a strong phone habit
- **Joseph sir**, 61, from Thottilpalam: a retired Malayalam teacher who runs a small study group at the panchayat library

## Other courses in this app

This course links to the others instead of repeating them:

- **Free AI Generalist Course:** how AI models work and why they make things up (Level 0), and prompting (Level 1). Module 17 here uses AI for studying; that course teaches AI as a skill.
- **Practical Entrepreneurship**, **Practical Social Media Marketing** and **Practical Personal Finance:** good next courses once your learning system runs (see **What next**). The methods you learn here apply to every one of them.

## A weekly rhythm that fits around PSC study

- **Every morning, 15 minutes:** AnkiDroid reviews (from week 4), before you open WhatsApp or YouTube.
- **Your main PSC study block:** use the method from the latest lesson on that day's PSC topic. This is where the course pays off.
- **Weekday evenings, 30–40 minutes:** read one lesson and do its quiz.
- **Saturday, 60–90 minutes:** the action task. Most need your books, question papers and a quiet hour.
- **Sunday, 20 minutes:** the weekly learning review and next week's plan.

## When you fall behind

- **This week** on the course page shows earlier open tasks as overdue. Do the action tasks first; readings can wait.
- More than two weeks behind? Set a new start date on the course page so the weeks match your real progress. Your ticks are kept.
- Use each module's "short on time?" version when you need it.
- Never skip the daily AnkiDroid reviews to catch up on lessons: missed reviews pile up (LRN-M04-L04).

## Exam mode

In the last four weeks before a PSC exam, pause new lessons. Keep AnkiDroid, the weekly review and your 12-week plan's final phase (LRN-M12-L05), and reread LRN-M12-L04 and LRN-M12-L06. Move your start date later by the same number of weeks. The course waits for you.

sections.title: Week 0: Learning Folder, Learning Workbook and your PSC material
sections.summary: One private folder, one workbook, your PSC syllabus and question papers, weekly slots, and two habits that start today.
sections.content:
Week 0 takes about 4 hours, including the baseline tests on the next page. You set up the places where your learning system will live, collect your PSC material, and measure where you start.

## 1. A Learning Folder

Make a folder called **Learning Folder** in Google Drive (or on your phone, if you prefer to keep it offline) with these subfolders: 00 Baseline, 01 Brain, 02 Myths, 03 Strategies, 04 Anki, 05 Focus, 06 Habits, 07 Metacognition, 08 Understanding, 09 Notes, 10 Reading, 11 Memory, 12 Exam, 13 Practice, 14 Maths, 15 Language, 16 Thinking, 17 AI, 18 Knowledge base, 19 Health, 20 Teaching, 21 Capstone. Every proof goes into one of them: photos of handwritten work, screenshots, voice recordings and filled-in templates.

Keep it **private**. Your recordings and scores are for you; share only what you choose.

## 2. The Learning Workbook

Make one spreadsheet called **Learning Workbook** in Google Sheets (phone or laptop). LibreOffice Calc on the laptop opens the same file if you prefer working offline. Start with three tabs; later modules add the rest:

| Tab | Added in | Row 1 headings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | Week 0 | `Your four baseline test scores and habit ratings, start and end` |
| Study Log | Week 0 | `Date,Subject,Topic,Minutes,Method,Focus (1-5),What I can now recall,Next step` |
| Weekly | Week 0 | `Week,Dates,Study hours,AnkiDroid days (of 7),AnkiDroid true retention %,Self-test score %,Mock or PYQ score,Focus blocks done,Top error type,One change for next week` |
| Revision | Module 3 | `Topic,First studied,Review 1 (+1 day),Review 2 (+3 days),Review 3 (+7 days),Review 4 (+21 days),Review 5 (+60 days),Next review,Due today?,Last score %` |
| Focus | Module 5 | `Date,Task,Planned minutes,Minutes to first distraction,Distractions (tally),Phone where?,Focus (1-10),Note` |
| Syllabus | Module 12 | `Subject,Topic (from the official syllabus),Marks or share,PYQ count,Confidence (1-5),Status (not started / learning / revising / solid),Source I use,Next review` |
| PYQ | Module 12 | `Paper (post and year),Question no,Subject,Topic,Subtopic,Type (fact / concept / calculation / statement),Repeated? (Y/N),Seen in my material? (Y/N),Right at first try? (Y/N),Notes` |
| Errors | Module 12 | `Date,Source (mock / PYQ / practice),Question no,Subject,Topic,My answer,Correct answer,Error type,Why it happened,Fix (card / note / rule),Retest date,Retest result` |
| Sprint | Module 21 | `Day,Date,Minutes,What I studied,Methods used,Retrieval score (e.g. 7/10),Cards added,Energy (1-5),Note` |

- **On the laptop:** paste a heading line into cell A1, then use **Data → Split text to columns** (Google Sheets) or **Data → Text to Columns** (LibreOffice).
- **On the phone:** type the headings into row 1, one per cell.
- **Formulas** in this course work in Google Sheets and LibreOffice Calc. If LibreOffice shows an error, change the commas between the parts of a formula to semicolons (its setting is under Tools → Options → LibreOffice Calc → Formula).

## 3. Your PSC material

Every action task uses your real material, so collect it now:

1. **Choose your target exam.** If you have several, choose the next big one.
2. **Download its syllabus** from the [Kerala PSC post-wise syllabus page](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/syllabus1) (check current rules) and save it in **12 Exam**.
3. **Download at least three previous question papers** for the same or a similar post from [Kerala PSC previous question papers](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/previous-question-papers), and their final answer keys from [the answer key page](https://www.keralapsc.gov.in/answerkey_omrexams).
4. **List your main sources** for each subject: SCERT school textbooks ([SCERT Kerala](https://scert.kerala.gov.in/)), any guide or rank file you already own, your notes, and one current-affairs source (Module 10 builds this).

## 4. Your phone and laptop

- Nothing new to install yet. You need the **Clock app** (stopwatch and timer) and a **voice recorder** (most phones have one; a voice note to yourself also works).
- Later modules install free, open-source apps: AnkiDroid (Module 4), Loop Habit Tracker (Module 6) and Joplin or Logseq (Module 18).
- Turn off notifications for games and shopping apps today. Module 5 goes much further.

## 5. Your weekly slots

Block about 6 hours a week in your calendar, outside your best PSC study hours: for example 35 minutes on five weekday evenings, 90 minutes on Saturday and 20 minutes on Sunday for the weekly review.

## 6. A helper and a study partner

Ask a family member or friend to help for 10 minutes with the digit-span test on the next page, and again in week 28. Ask a friend or classmate who also studies for PSC whether they'd be your study partner for Module 20; it helps from the start to have someone to quiz.

## 7. An AI tutor (optional)

The free plans of common AI chat tools can quiz you and explain ideas. Save this prompt and paste it at the start of a study chat:

```
You are my study tutor for the Kerala PSC exam. I am a beginner at learning
techniques, and I study in English with Malayalam as my first language.
Today's topic: [topic]. My goal for this session: [goal].
1. Ask me 2-3 questions first to find out what I already know.
2. Do not give me long answers. Teach one small idea at a time, then ask me a
   question that makes me recall or explain it.
3. If I am wrong, give a hint before giving the answer.
4. At the end, quiz me with 5 questions in PSC style, then list what I should
   review.
5. If you are not sure a fact is correct, say so, and tell me which official
   source or textbook to check.
```

AI tools can be confidently wrong about PSC facts. Check facts against your textbook or an official source, and let the AI question you rather than do the thinking for you (Module 17).

## 8. Start two habits today

- **The study log:** after every study session, add one row to the **Study Log** tab: what you studied, for how long, which method, and one thing you can now recall without looking. It takes one minute and builds the data for your weekly reviews.
- **The weekly review:** every Sunday, answer three questions in a notebook or the **Weekly** tab: What did I learn (from memory)? What worked? What will I change? The full version arrives in LRN-M07-L03.

Every link on this page was checked on 2026-11-03. The **Sources and verification log** at the end of the course lists each one with its status.

sections.summary: Four short tests and a habits rating to measure where you start: list recall after 10 minutes and 24 hours, reading speed with comprehension, focus duration and digit span. You repeat them in week 28.

Before you learn anything new, measure where you start. These four short tests and a habits rating take about 1.5 hours, spread over two days, because two of them need a second session. In week 28 you repeat them with fresh versions (form B, on the final page), so you can see what changed. Don't practise for them, and don't look at form B.

Copy this table into the **Baseline** tab of your Learning Workbook and fill in the **Start** column as you go:

| Test | Start (week 0) | End (week 28) | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| List recall after 10 minutes (out of 20) |  |  |  |
| List recall after 24 hours (out of 20) |  |  |  |
| Reading speed (words per minute) |  |  |  |
| Comprehension (out of 8, and %) |  |  |  |
| Effective reading rate (wpm × comprehension %) |  |  |  |
| Minutes to first distraction (average of 2 days) |  |  |  |
| Distractions in 45 minutes (average of 2 days) |  |  |  |
| Digit span forward |  |  |  |
| Digit span backward |  |  |  |
| Learning habits total (out of 75) |  |  |  |

## Test 1: the 20-item list (about 20 minutes, plus 3 minutes tomorrow)

1. Have a pen, paper and a timer ready. Set the timer for **2 minutes**.
2. Start the timer and study the list below in any way you like. Stop when the timer rings.
3. Cover the list. For the next **10 minutes**, do something that keeps your mind busy, such as arithmetic questions from your PSC book. Don't rehearse the list.
4. Write down every word you remember, in any order, in **3 minutes**. Count the correct words (spelling doesn't matter). That is your **10-minute score**.
5. **Don't look at the list again.** Exactly 24 hours later, write the words again in 3 minutes, without looking. That is your **24-hour score**.

```
LIST A (study for 2 minutes)
 1. umbrella
 2. tiger
 3. candle
 4. onion
 5. bicycle
 6. newspaper
 7. drum
 8. mango
 9. ladder
10. pillow
11. key
12. bucket
13. elephant
14. scissors
15. boat
16. mirror
17. rope
18. coconut
19. kite
20. bottle
```

## Test 2: reading speed and comprehension (about 15 minutes)

1. Read the passage below **once**, at your normal pace for understanding: not skimming, not studying. Time yourself with the stopwatch from the first word to the last.
2. Without looking back, answer the 8 questions below it.
3. Work out your scores:
    - **Reading speed (wpm)** = 543 words ÷ your minutes. Example: 3 minutes 20 seconds is 3.33 minutes, so 543 ÷ 3.33 = 163 wpm.
    - **Comprehension %** = correct answers ÷ 8 × 100
    - **Effective reading rate** = wpm × comprehension % ÷ 100

### Passage A: The reading room at Puthenpura (543 words)

Puthenpura is a small village on the bank of a slow, brown river. For many years it had a post office, two tea shops, a mosque, a temple and a school that went up to class seven, but no place where an adult could sit and read. Devaki, a mathematics teacher who retired in 1998, decided to change that.

She began with what she had: forty-two books from her own shelves and a promise from the owner of an empty ration shop near the bus stop. He let her use the room for nothing, on one condition: it had to be swept every day and locked every night. Devaki wrote the rules on a sheet of chart paper and pinned it beside the door. Members would pay two rupees a month. Books could be taken home for one week. Anyone who returned a book late would have to read a page of it aloud to the others on Sunday evening.

In the first month only nine people joined. Most of them were retired men who came for the newspaper, not the books. Devaki did not mind. She noticed that they argued every morning about the news, so she started a small notebook in which anyone could write one question about the day's paper. Every Saturday, she pinned the best question on the wall with the answer underneath. Within a few months, the notebook had become the most read item in the room.

The first real problem came during the monsoon of 1999. The room flooded twice, and termites attacked the wooden shelves. About a third of the books were damaged. A carpenter from the next village suggested raising the shelves on bricks and painting the legs with old engine oil. Devaki's former students collected money for the bricks and the paint, and the shelves have stood on the same bricks ever since.

The second change came from an unexpected direction. In 2001 the bus timetable changed, and the last bus to the town now left at seven in the evening instead of five. Women who worked in the town's tailoring shops had a long wait at the bus stop, right outside the reading room. A few of them began to step in while they waited. Devaki started a Thursday group for them, in which each person read one short story and then told it to the others in her own words. By the end of that year, membership had grown to more than eighty, and for the first time most members were women.

Not everything worked. A plan to lend books by post to people in the hills was dropped after a year, because the stamps cost more than the fees. A computer donated in 2006 sat unused for a long time, since no one knew how to repair it when the power supply failed.

Today the reading room has about two thousand books, a wall of old question notebooks and a waiting list for the Thursday group. Devaki still visits on Sundays. When young people ask her how she built it, she says that she did not build anything. "I opened the door," she says, "and then I watched what people did when they came in, and gave them more of that."

### Questions on passage A

1. Where did the reading room first open?
    - A) In a room of the village school
    - B) In Devaki's house
    - C) Beside the post office
    - D) In an empty ration shop near the bus stop
2. What did a member who returned a book late have to do?
    - A) Sweep the room for a week
    - B) Pay a fine of two rupees
    - C) Read a page of it aloud on Sunday evening
    - D) Give up borrowing for a month
3. What became the most read item in the room within a few months?
    - A) The chart of rules
    - B) The newspaper itself
    - C) A book of short stories
    - D) The notebook of questions about the day's newspaper
4. How were the shelves protected after the 1999 monsoon?
    - A) They were replaced with steel shelves
    - B) They were wrapped in plastic sheets
    - C) They were moved to a higher room
    - D) They were raised on bricks and the legs painted with old engine oil
5. Why did more women start using the reading room in 2001?
    - A) A change in the bus timetable left them waiting right outside it
    - B) The fee was cut for women
    - C) Devaki put up notices in the tailoring shops
    - D) The school asked them to come
6. Why was the plan to lend books by post dropped?
    - A) People in the hills did not want books
    - B) Books were lost in the post
    - C) The stamps cost more than the fees
    - D) The post office closed
7. Which statement best matches Devaki's own view of how the reading room grew?
    - A) She followed a detailed plan written in 1998
    - B) The donated computer brought in new members
    - C) Her former students did most of the work
    - D) She watched what members did and gave them more of it
8. Which of these is NOT stated in the passage?
    - A) Membership passed eighty by the end of 2001
    - B) The donated computer was unused after its power supply failed
    - C) The reading room received a government grant
    - D) Devaki was a mathematics teacher

## Test 3: focus duration (45 minutes, on two different days)

1. Choose a normal PSC study task: reading a new chapter and making notes works well.
2. Set up the way you **usually** study. Don't change anything for the test.
3. Start the stopwatch. Study for 45 minutes. Keep a paper beside you: every time you notice your attention left the task (you checked the phone, got up, started daydreaming), make a tally mark. Write down the time of the **first** one.
4. Record: **minutes to first distraction**, **number of tally marks**, and a focus rating from 1 to 10.
5. Repeat on another day this week, and use the average of the two.

## Test 4: digit span (10 minutes, with a helper if possible)

**With a helper (best):** the helper reads each line aloud at about one digit per second, in a flat voice. You repeat the digits (forward: same order; backward: reverse order). Start at the shortest lines. Stop a section when you fail **both** lines of the same length.

**Alone:** cover the list with a paper and slide it down to show one line for as many seconds as there are digits, cover it again, and write the digits down. Use the same method again in week 28, so the scores compare fairly.

**Your span** in each section is the longest length where you got at least one of the two lines exactly right.

```
DIGIT SPAN, FORM A
FORWARD (say them back in the same order)
3 digits: 4 1 6
3 digits: 4 7 0
4 digits: 0 4 1 7
4 digits: 4 1 6 2
5 digits: 9 3 1 6 0
5 digits: 4 8 0 7 3
6 digits: 4 1 3 9 5 8
6 digits: 4 9 3 1 8 2
7 digits: 0 9 5 2 6 4 8
7 digits: 0 6 1 5 2 7 4
8 digits: 7 0 5 2 8 4 9 1
8 digits: 5 8 2 4 1 6 0 7
9 digits: 9 1 5 2 6 8 0 3 7
9 digits: 6 2 7 0 8 4 9 3 1

BACKWARD (say them back in reverse order)
2 digits: 2 9
2 digits: 8 0
3 digits: 0 4 7
3 digits: 4 9 7
4 digits: 3 9 0 6
4 digits: 3 6 2 9
5 digits: 8 6 0 2 7
5 digits: 2 8 3 9 7
6 digits: 8 2 7 9 1 3
6 digits: 3 8 1 5 2 7
7 digits: 0 4 6 1 5 2 9
7 digits: 2 7 3 1 5 0 6
8 digits: 5 7 0 8 1 6 9 4
8 digits: 8 1 9 2 0 5 3 7
```

## Part 5: your learning habits (5 minutes)

Rate each statement: **1** never, **2** rarely, **3** sometimes, **4** usually, **5** almost always. Add them up (out of 75).

| No | Statement | Start | End |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | When I study, I test myself more than I reread |  |  |
| 2 | I review topics on a schedule, not only just before an exam |  |  |
| 3 | I mix different types of questions when I practise |  |  |
| 4 | I explain ideas in my own words, aloud or on paper |  |  |
| 5 | I use pictures, maps, timelines or diagrams with my notes |  |  |
| 6 | I review flashcards with spaced repetition every day |  |  |
| 7 | I can study for 45 minutes without checking my phone |  |  |
| 8 | I start study sessions on time, without long delays |  |  |
| 9 | I know which topics I really know and which I only recognise |  |  |
| 10 | I keep a record of my mistakes and fix them |  |  |
| 11 | I practise with previous-year questions and timed tests |  |  |
| 12 | I sleep at least 7 hours on most nights |  |  |
| 13 | I have a written study plan for my exam |  |  |
| 14 | I can learn a new skill on my own with free resources |  |  |
| 15 | I check facts from AI tools or social media against a reliable source |  |  |

## Answer key for passage A

Check only after you have answered all 8 questions: **1D, 2C, 3D, 4D, 5A, 6C, 7D, 8C**.

## What your scores mean

There are no good or bad scores here; they are your starting line. Short-term memory holds roughly seven items, give or take two ([OpenStax Psychology 2e, 8.1](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/8-1-how-memory-functions)), so a 20-word list is meant to be too long to hold without a method. What matters is the change by week 28, and the methods you used to get it. Save a photo of your answer sheets and a screenshot of the Baseline tab in **00 Baseline**.

sections.title: Learning system track: weekly reviews and the 30-day AnkiDroid review
sections.summary: A 20-minute review every Sunday from week 1, and daily AnkiDroid reviews for 30 days from week 4. Eleven checkpoints keep you on track.
sections.content:
Two habits run underneath the whole course. They turn lessons into a system. **This week** on the course page shows the checkpoints when they are due.

## Habit 1: the weekly learning review (every Sunday, from week 1)

Twenty minutes, at the same time every week. Until you reach LRN-M07-L03, use the short version:

1. **Recall:** without notes, write the three most important things you learned this week.
2. **Numbers:** hours studied, days of AnkiDroid done (from week 4), and any test score.
3. **Adjust:** what worked, what didn't, and one change for next week.

From week 8, use the full **weekly review** template (it is also on the **Toolkit** page) and copy its numbers into the **Weekly** tab.

## Habit 2: the 30-day AnkiDroid review (from week 4)

In Module 4 you build a deck of 100 or more cards on one PSC topic. The course asks you to review it **every day for 30 days**. That proves the habit, and it is long enough to see spaced repetition work.

- **Review every day,** even on bad days: 5 minutes is better than none. Do the reviews before you add new cards.
- **Count review days, not calendar days.** If you miss a day, the 30 days end a day later.
- **Add new cards gradually:** about 10 to 20 new cards a day until the deck has 100 or more (LRN-M04-L04 explains the workload).
- **Proof:** a screenshot of the AnkiDroid statistics screen with its calendar, and your true retention (the share of mature reviews you passed).

## Checkpoints

| Due by week | Checkpoint | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Weekly learning review (week 1) | Weekly tab row and your written review |
| 4 | Weekly learning review (week 4) | Weekly tab row and your written review |
| 5 | AnkiDroid: day 7 of 30 reviewed | Screenshot of the AnkiDroid statistics calendar |
| 6 | AnkiDroid: day 14 of 30 reviewed | Screenshot of the AnkiDroid statistics calendar |
| 7 | AnkiDroid: day 21 of 30 reviewed | Screenshot of the AnkiDroid statistics calendar |
| 8 | Weekly learning review (week 8) | Weekly tab row and your written review |
| 8 | AnkiDroid: day 30 of 30 reviewed | Screenshot of the AnkiDroid statistics calendar |
| 12 | Weekly learning review (week 12) | Weekly tab row and your written review |
| 16 | Weekly learning review (week 16) | Weekly tab row and your written review |
| 20 | Weekly learning review (week 20) | Weekly tab row and your written review |
| 24 | Weekly learning review (week 24) | Weekly tab row and your written review |

## When a checkpoint is missed

Missing one is information, not failure. Ask why: no fixed time, too many new cards, exam pressure, a bad week? Fix that one thing. Never try to "catch up" weeks of reviews in one sitting; do today's, and the backlog clears in a few days (LRN-M04-L04).

These are the six core tools of your learning system, in one place, ready to copy into your notebook, Joplin or the Learning Workbook. Each was introduced in a lesson; the lesson explains how to use it well.

## Study planner

From LRN-M05-L02 (time-blocking) and LRN-M12-L05 (the 12-week plan).

```
WEEKLY STUDY PLANNER          Week of: ________
Exam: __________________ on ________   Weeks left: ___
Hours this week: course ___ + PSC study ___ = ___

DAY   BLOCK (time)   SUBJECT : TOPIC            METHOD                    DONE
Mon   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Tue   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Wed   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Thu   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Fri   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Sat   ____–____      ________ : __________      ______________________    [ ]
Sun   20 minutes     Weekly learning review + plan next week               [ ]

METHOD words: retrieval (blank-page recall, practice questions), spaced review
(from the Revision tab), mixed practice (interleaving), Feynman, cards, mock test.

Every day:  [ ] AnkiDroid reviews (___ min)  [ ] one retrieval session
            [ ] phone in another room during blocks  [ ] sleep by ____
If-then plans: If ____________________, then I will ____________________.
```

## Revision schedule

From LRN-M03-L02 (spaced practice).

```
REVISION SCHEDULE (expanding gaps)
Day 0   Learn it: read, understand, make notes and questions
Day 1   Review 1: blank-page recall, then check and fix
Day 3   Review 2: answer your questions from memory
Day 7   Review 3: mixed practice questions with other topics
Day 21  Review 4: PYQs or a short timed test on this topic
Day 60  Review 5: quick recall; anything you miss goes to AnkiDroid
Every review starts with RECALL, not rereading. Score yourself, and log the
score in the Revision tab. A score under 60% means: re-learn the gaps and
restart the schedule from Day 1 for that topic.
Facts (names, dates, articles, numbers) live in AnkiDroid, which spaces them
for you. This schedule is for whole topics and skills.
```

## Card-writing checklist

From LRN-M04-L02 (writing good cards).

```
CARD-WRITING CHECKLIST (tick before you add a card)
[ ] I understand it: I could explain it in my own words
[ ] One fact per card (the minimum information principle)
[ ] The question has exactly one correct answer
[ ] The answer is short: a word, a number, a name or a phrase
[ ] Lists are split: one cloze per item, or a memory palace instead
[ ] A context cue starts the question when needed ("Constitution:", "Kerala rivers:")
[ ] Look-alike facts are made clearly different ("longest" vs "largest")
[ ] A picture, map or diagram is used where it helps (image occlusion)
[ ] The source is in the Source field (book and page, or PYQ paper and number)
[ ] It is worth knowing: it is on the syllabus or has appeared in PYQs
```

## Error log

From LRN-M12-L03 (mock tests and the error log).

```
ERROR LOG (one row per wrong or guessed question; Errors tab)
Date | Source | Q no | Subject | Topic | My answer | Correct | Type | Why | Fix | Retest date | Retest result
Error types:
K = didn't know      F = forgot         I = interference (mixed up two facts)
M = misread          C = careless slip  G = bad guess      T = ran out of time
Fix rules:
K or F -> make 1-3 cards, or add the topic to the Revision tab
I      -> one card that contrasts the two facts side by side
M      -> underline NOT / EXCEPT / FIRST / LARGEST in every question for a week
C      -> slow down on the last step; check the OMR bubble number
G      -> guess only after ruling out at least one option
T      -> two-pass method in the next mock
Retest every error 7 days later, from memory. Clear it only when it is right twice.
```

## Feynman template

From LRN-M08-L01 (self-explanation and the Feynman technique).

```
FEYNMAN EXPLANATION       Topic: ______________   Date: ________
Recording: v1 file ________  v2 file ________
1. Explain it aloud, without notes, to an imaginary 12-year-old (2-3 minutes).
   Record it on your phone (v1).
2. Listen back. Mark every gap: where I stopped, said "basically" or "something
   like", used a word I can't define, or got a fact wrong:
   ___________________________________________________________________
3. Go back to the source (book ______ page ___). Fix each gap:
   ___________________________________________________________________
4. Simplify: one analogy or example from Kerala life: ____________________
5. Record again without notes (v2). What is clearer now? __________________
6. Turn the gaps into 2-3 flashcards and 1 question for my Revision tab.
Score each 1-3:  Accuracy __  Clarity __  Complete __  Without notes __  Total __/12
```

## Weekly review

From LRN-M07-L03 (the weekly learning review).

```
WEEKLY LEARNING REVIEW        Week ___ (dates ________)   20 minutes, Sunday
Numbers: study hours ___ | AnkiDroid days ___/7, true retention ___%
         self-test ___% | mock or PYQ score ___ | focus blocks ___
1. From memory, no notes: the three most important things I learned this week
   ______________________________________________________________________
2. Cold self-test: 5 questions from this week's topics. Score ___/5
3. Calibration: what did I feel sure about but get wrong? ________________
4. Error log: my most common error type this week ___ ; the fix ___________
5. What worked? ______________________  What didn't? ______________________
6. Next week's three priorities, each with a day and time (if-then plans)
   1. ________________ 2. ________________ 3. ________________
7. One change to my system: ______________________________________________
Copy the numbers into the Weekly tab of the Learning Workbook.
```

```
In row 2, with the first study date in B2 (type it as a date, e.g. 2026-11-09):
C2: =B2+1
D2: =B2+3
E2: =B2+7
F2: =B2+21

H2: =IF(C2>=TODAY(),C2,IF(D2>=TODAY(),D2,IF(E2>=TODAY(),E2,IF(F2>=TODAY(),F2,IF(G2>=TODAY(),G2,"done")))))
I2: =IF(OR(C2=TODAY(),D2=TODAY(),E2=TODAY(),F2=TODAY(),G2=TODAY()),"DUE","")
Format C2:H2 as dates. Copy row 2 down for every new topic. Sort or filter by column H to see what is coming.
```

## Error types

| --- | --- |
| K | Didn't know: never learned it, or not on my cards |
| F | Forgot: learned it once, could not recall it in time |
| I | Interference: mixed it up with a similar fact |
| M | Misread: missed a word such as NOT, first, largest, except |
| C | Careless: a slip in calculation or in marking the OMR bubble |
| G | Bad guess: guessed when I could not rule anything out |

sections.title: Module 1: How your brain learns
sections.summary: Learn how attention, working memory, encoding, sleep, retrieval and forgetting work, and test each idea on your own PSC facts. Three small experiments in your first week show you why the rest of the course works.
sections.content:
## Overview

You don't need biology to learn well, but a simple model of your mind explains almost every method in this course. Working memory is small, so you chunk and remove distractions. Meaning makes memories last, so you ask why. Sleep consolidates memories, so you protect it. Retrieval strengthens memory and forgetting is fast, so you recall instead of rereading and you review on a schedule.

Each lesson ends with an experiment on your real PSC material. By Sunday you will have your own evidence, not just someone else's.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain attention, working memory, long-term memory and cognitive load, and reduce the load of a hard page
- Explain encoding, consolidation and neuroplasticity, and encode facts through meaning
- Explain the forgetting curve and the testing effect
- Show with your own data that recall beats rereading
- Draw a one-page model of how you learn, with three personal rules

## Time

About 4 hours 45 minutes in total: 3 hours 45 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: week 1, with the module project due in week 1.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M01-L01: Attention, working memory and cognitive load (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M01-L02: Encoding, consolidation, sleep and neuroplasticity (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
3. LRN-M01-L03: Retrieval and the forgetting curve (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **Study Log** tab, now with a "Method" column you fill in every session
- The **cognitive load audit** for hard pages
- The **blank-page recall routine** you will use after every reading session
- The **7-night sleep log**

## Module project: My one-page learning model

1. On one page, draw the path from attention to working memory to long-term memory. Add encoding, consolidation (sleep), retrieval and forgetting, with arrows. Use your own words and small pictures.
2. Next to it, write the results of your three experiments: the load audit, the encoding experiment and recall versus reread.
3. Write your three personal study rules for the coming month, each based on one result (for example: "Phone in the kitchen during study", "Ask why for every fact", "Five minutes of recall after every reading").
4. Explain the page aloud to someone at home in under three minutes.

**Proof to record:** A photo of your one-page model with the three experiment results and your three rules.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Model | Missing parts or copied from the book | All parts, with some unclear links | All parts in your own words, with arrows and examples |
| Experiments | None run | One or two run | All three run and recorded |
| Rules | Vague ("study better") | Specific but not based on results | Three specific rules, each linked to a result |
| Explaining | Could not explain it | Explained with the page in hand | Explained in under three minutes, page face down |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Read Nicky Case's comic.
- Do only the recall-versus-reread experiment (LRN-M01-L03).
- Write one rule: five minutes of blank-page recall after every reading session.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

sections.title: LRN-M01-L01: Attention, working memory and cognitive load
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain why attention and working memory limit how fast you learn, and cut the load of one hard PSC page so it becomes learnable. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 35 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Everything you learn for PSC takes the same path through your mind:

1. **Attention** picks what you work on. Whatever you don't attend to, you don't learn. A phone that buzzes every few minutes keeps pulling attention away.
2. **Working memory** holds what you are thinking about right now, while you make sense of it. It is like a small desk: only a few things fit at once.
3. **Long-term memory** is the huge store of what you know. Learning means getting knowledge from the desk into this store, organised so you can find it again.

This is the classic three-store model of memory, explained in [OpenStax Psychology 2e, section 8.1](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/8-1-how-memory-functions).

### The desk is small

Working memory is tiny and short-lived. Without rehearsal, information in short-term memory fades in about 15 to 30 seconds. The old estimate was that it holds about seven items, give or take two; newer research puts the limit nearer four "chunks" (OpenStax 8.1; [NSW CESE review of cognitive load theory](https://education.nsw.gov.au/content/dam/main-education/about-us/educational-data/cese/2017-cognitive-load-theory.pdf)).

That is why a dense page in a PSC guide can feel impossible. Eight new names, five dates and three article numbers arrive together, and the desk overflows. You read the page, turn it, and almost nothing remains.

### Long-term memory changes the size of the desk

Long-term memory has no practical limit, and it stores knowledge in organised patterns called **schemas**. When you already know something well, it takes up almost no space on the desk. If you know multiplication tables by heart, a percentage problem uses your working memory for the reasoning, not for "7 × 8". If you already know the structure of the Constitution (Parts, Articles, Schedules), a new fact about Article 21A has somewhere to go.

So the more you know, the easier new learning becomes. Beginners need smaller steps; experts can take bigger ones.

### Cognitive load: what fills the desk

**Cognitive load** is how much a task demands from working memory. Two kinds matter for you:

- **Load from the material itself.** Centre-State relations, compound interest or Malayalam sandhi rules are hard because many ideas interact. You can't remove this load, but you can split it into smaller pieces.
- **Load from how you study.** A phone on the table, a guide that puts the answers on another page, notes in three different notebooks, unknown English words, noise from the TV. This load adds nothing to learning. Remove as much of it as you can.

### What this means for your study

- **One thing at a time.** Study one chunk, check you have it, then move on.
- **Split hard pages** into 3 to 5 chunks of one idea each.
- **Worked examples first, for beginners.** In maths and reasoning, study a fully solved example step by step before solving alone. Beginners who study worked examples do better on later tests than those who struggle with problems unaided (the "worked example effect" in the CESE review). As you improve, switch to solving on your own: the same review describes this "expertise reversal".
- **Build background knowledge.** Basic facts in long-term memory (tables, key dates, the structure of the Constitution) make everything else easier. That is why Module 4 puts them into AnkiDroid.
- **Don't buy "brain training".** Apps that promise to enlarge working memory make you better at the app's own games, but a large review of 87 publications found no convincing gains in reading, arithmetic or intelligence ([Melby-Lervåg, Redick and Hulme, 2016](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:daa9a729-f17b-4e45-97c0-cff5075ea404)).

## Local example

**Sreeja** studies in Nadapuram in two 45-minute slots, one while her children are at school and one after they sleep. Her guide's page on Centre-State relations has three lists, a dozen article numbers and two tables. She read it four times in a week and still mixed up the lists.

She did a load audit of her last session. From the setup: the phone was face-up on the table (seven WhatsApp notifications), the TV was on in the next room, and she kept flipping to the end of the guide for the meaning of "concurrent". From the material: three lists with similar names.

She changed the setup first: the phone went into the bedroom, she wrote the five unknown words on a slip of paper beside the book, and she used the morning slot, when the house is quiet. Then she split the page into four chunks: legislative relations, administrative relations, financial relations, and the three lists. For each chunk she read, closed the book, wrote two lines from memory and checked.

The page that had taken four readings took one 40-minute session. She rated its difficulty 8 out of 10 before and 5 after. The material hadn't changed; the load had.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Working memory is small (a few chunks) and brief | **Strong** | A core finding of memory research, summarised in OpenStax Psychology 2e and the CESE review. |
| Worked examples help beginners; problem solving helps once you are skilled | **Strong** | The worked example and expertise reversal effects, described in the CESE review of cognitive load theory. |
| Removing distractions and split sources lowers load | **Moderate** | Consistent with cognitive load research; your own load audit is the best test of what distracts you. |
| Working memory training apps make you smarter | **No good evidence** | Melby-Lervåg and others (2016): short-term, narrow gains with no convincing transfer to reading, arithmetic or intelligence. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, 8.1 How Memory Functions](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/8-1-how-memory-functions) | Read the parts on the three memory stores (sensory, short-term, long-term) and short-term memory | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [NSW Centre for Education Statistics and Evaluation (2017), "Cognitive load theory: Research that teachers really need to understand" (PDF)](https://education.nsw.gov.au/content/dam/main-education/about-us/educational-data/cese/2017-cognitive-load-theory.pdf) | Read the sections on working memory, long-term memory and the worked example effect | 25 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Melby-Lervåg, Redick and Hulme (2016): working memory training does not improve far transfer](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:daa9a729-f17b-4e45-97c0-cff5075ea404) | Read the abstract only: what working memory training can and cannot do | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Pick the hardest page or section in the PSC subject you are studying this week: a dense GK page, a Constitution topic or a maths chapter.
2. Do a load audit of the last time you studied it, with the template below. Mark each item as "material" or "setup".
3. Remove at least two setup loads before your next session: for example, phone in another room, unknown words on a slip beside the book, answers on the same page as the questions.
4. Split the page into 3 to 5 chunks of one idea each. For each chunk: read it, close the book, write one or two lines from memory, then check and correct in a different colour.
5. If it is a maths or reasoning topic: study one worked example step by step, cover it, solve the same problem yourself, then solve one similar problem.
6. Rate the difficulty of the page from 1 to 10 before and after, and add a row to your Study Log.

**Proof to record:** A photo of your load audit and the chunked page with your one-line recalls, and the Study Log row.

## Template: cognitive load audit

```
COGNITIVE LOAD AUDIT      Page / topic: ______________   Date: ______
Difficulty before (1-10): ___

What competed for my working memory?          Material or setup?   Fix
1. ____________________________________       ________             ______________
2. ____________________________________       ________             ______________
3. ____________________________________       ________             ______________
4. ____________________________________       ________             ______________

Chunks (one idea each):
1. ______________  my 2-line recall: ________________________  checked [ ]
2. ______________  my 2-line recall: ________________________  checked [ ]
3. ______________  my 2-line recall: ________________________  checked [ ]
4. ______________  my 2-line recall: ________________________  checked [ ]

Difficulty after (1-10): ___   Time taken: ___ minutes
```

## Template: Study Log headings (if you have not made the tab yet)

```csv
Date,Subject,Topic,Minutes,Method,Focus (1-5),What I can now recall,Next step
```

## Common mistakes

- **Studying with the phone face-up.** Every notification takes a piece of your small desk. Put it in another room during study blocks; Module 5 goes further.
- **Trying to swallow a whole chapter in one go.** Split it into chunks of one idea and check each one from memory before moving on.
- **Attacking hard maths problems with no worked example.** Study a fully solved example first, then solve. Switch to solving alone once the steps feel easy.
- **Rereading a page that overloads you.** Rereading adds the same overload again. Reduce the load first, then recall.
- **Paying for "brain training" apps.** They train the app, not your exam skills. Spend the time on your syllabus.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. According to newer research, about how many chunks can working memory hold at once?
    - A) About four
    - B) Exactly one
    - C) An unlimited number
    - D) About forty
2. Which of these is load from how you study, which you can remove?
    - A) Flipping between the questions and an answer key at the back of the book
    - B) The number of ideas in Centre-State relations
    - C) The fact that compound interest has several steps
    - D) The length of the syllabus
3. You are new to percentages. What should you do first?
    - A) Attempt 50 hard problems with no help
    - B) Study a worked example step by step, then solve a similar problem
    - C) Watch a speed-maths video
    - D) Read the theory three times
4. What did a large review find about working memory training apps?
    - A) They raise IQ by 10 points
    - B) Gains on trained tasks, but no convincing transfer to reading, arithmetic or intelligence
    - C) They double reading speed
    - D) They work only for children

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax 8.1 on the memory stores and the CESE review sections on working memory and worked examples
- **Action:** Audit and chunk one hard PSC page, and log the session. It is done when your proof is saved: a photo of your load audit and the chunked page with your one-line recalls, and the Study Log row.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** Newer estimates put the limit near four chunks; the older estimate was about seven, give or take two.
2. **A.** Split sources add load without adding learning. Put questions and answers together.
3. **B.** The worked example effect: beginners learn more from studying solved examples first.
4. **B.** Melby-Lervåg and others (2016) reviewed 87 publications and found narrow, short-term effects.

sections.title: LRN-M01-L02: Encoding, consolidation, sleep and neuroplasticity
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain how memories are made and stabilised, encode PSC facts through meaning instead of repetition, and protect the sleep that consolidates them. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 30 minutes action plus a 7-night sleep log).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Encoding: getting it in

**Encoding** is turning what you read or hear into a memory. Not all encoding is equal. Repeating "Article 21, life and liberty, Article 21, life and liberty" keeps it on the desk for a while; psychologists call that **maintenance rehearsal**. Connecting it to meaning lasts much longer: **elaborative rehearsal** ([OpenStax Psychology 2e, 8.1](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/8-1-how-memory-functions)).

Compare two ways to learn that Article 21 protects life and personal liberty:

- **Repetition:** say "21: life and personal liberty" ten times.
- **Meaning:** ask "why is this right so important?" It protects you from losing your life or freedom except by procedure established by law, and courts have read many other rights into it, such as the right to live with dignity. Link it to something you know: a news story about an illegal detention. Picture a 21-year-old walking free out of a prison gate.

The second way takes a minute longer and is remembered far better, because it gives the fact many hooks in long-term memory. Everything in Module 3 (elaboration, concrete examples, dual coding) is a way to encode through meaning.

### Consolidation: making it stick

A new memory is fragile. Over the following hours, and especially during sleep, the brain stabilises it; this is **consolidation**. Sleep researchers have linked parts of sleep, including the sleep spindles of stage 2 and REM sleep, to learning and memory ([OpenStax Psychology 2e, 4.3](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/4-3-stages-of-sleep)). In a careful repeat of Ebbinghaus's forgetting experiment, Murre and Dros (2015) even saw memory scores jump upward at the 24-hour point, which they suggest may be an effect of sleep, though it is not proven ([PLOS ONE](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0120644)).

The practical message is simple:

- **Adults need 7 hours of sleep or more a night, regularly.** Less is linked with impaired performance and more errors ([AASM and Sleep Research Society consensus](https://www.aasm.org/resources/pdf/adultsleepdurationconsensus.pdf)).
- **An all-nighter before an exam trades memory for time.** You gain hours of reading and lose the consolidation of what you read.
- **Sleep after learning is part of learning.** A short recall of the day's topic before bed is a sensible habit, though the research on the best timing is limited.

### Neuroplasticity: you can still change your brain

**Neuroplasticity** is the brain's ability to change with learning and experience. It is greatest in early childhood, but substantial change continues in adults ([OpenStax Psychology 2e, 3.4](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/3-4-the-brain-and-spinal-cord)). In one study, adults with ordinary memories trained the memory palace for six weeks; their memory improved and their brain networks changed towards those of memory champions ([Dresler and others, 2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5439266/)).

At 30, 40 or 60 you can learn a subject, a language or a skill from zero. What changes with age is mostly how much time and practice you can give it, not whether learning is possible.

## Local example

**Ashiq**, 22, used to study until 2 a.m. with YouTube running in another tab, then slept until 9. He believed night study suited him.

He tried a small experiment on the Fundamental Rights. He learned five articles by repeating them, and five by meaning: for each he wrote one line on why it matters and linked it to something he knew (Article 17, the abolition of untouchability, to the temple-entry movements he had studied in Kerala history). The next morning he recalled 2 of the repeated five and 5 of the meaningful five.

Then he kept a sleep log for a week. He averaged under 6 hours, with a different bedtime every night. He moved his last study block to 9 p.m., did a 5-minute recall of the day's topic at 10:45, and put the phone on the charger in the kitchen at 11. After two weeks his average was 7 hours 20 minutes, and his morning recall scores were steadier. One week is not a scientific study, but it was enough to convince him.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Encoding through meaning beats repetition | **Strong** | Elaborative rehearsal and meaning-based encoding are well established (OpenStax 8.1); Dunlosky rates elaborative interrogation and self-explanation as promising study methods. |
| Enough sleep protects learning and performance | **Strong** | AASM and SRS consensus: adults need 7 or more hours; less is linked with impaired performance and errors. |
| Sleep stages help consolidate memories | **Moderate** | Spindles and REM sleep are linked to learning and memory (OpenStax 4.3); exactly how is still being researched. |
| Reviewing just before sleep is the best timing | **Limited** | Plausible and harmless, but the research on precise timing is limited. Judge it by your own morning recall. |
| Adult brains change with training | **Strong** | OpenStax 3.4 on neuroplasticity; Dresler and others (2017) on adults who trained the method of loci. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, 8.1 How Memory Functions](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/8-1-how-memory-functions) | Read the part on encoding, including semantic encoding and maintenance versus elaborative rehearsal | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, 4.3 Stages of Sleep](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/4-3-stages-of-sleep) | Read the stages of sleep, noting what each stage is linked to | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [AASM and Sleep Research Society (2015): recommended sleep for adults (PDF)](https://www.aasm.org/resources/pdf/adultsleepdurationconsensus.pdf) | Read the one-page recommendation for adults | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax Psychology 2e, 3.4 The Brain and Spinal Cord](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/3-4-the-brain-and-spinal-cord) | Read the paragraph on neuroplasticity | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose 10 new facts from your current PSC topic: for example 10 Fundamental Rights articles, 10 Kerala river facts or 10 Jnanpith winners with years.
2. Learn 5 of them by repetition only: read and repeat each one for one minute.
3. Learn the other 5 by meaning: for each, write one line on why it matters, link it to something you already know, or draw a tiny picture. Spend about one minute on each.
4. Next morning, after sleep and before looking at anything, write all 10 from memory. Score each group out of 5.
5. Keep a 7-night sleep log: time in bed, time up, hours slept, and how rested you feel (1 to 5).
6. Write one change for next week based on your log, such as a fixed bedtime, the phone charging outside the bedroom, or a 5-minute recall before bed.

**Proof to record:** Your 10-fact experiment with both scores, and the 7-night sleep log with your one change.

## Template: encoding experiment

```
ENCODING EXPERIMENT     Topic: ______________   Date learned: ______

REPETITION ONLY (1 minute each)        MEANING (1 minute each: why / link / picture)
1. ____________________________        6. ____________________________
2. ____________________________           why or link: _________________
3. ____________________________        7. ____________________________
4. ____________________________           why or link: _________________
5. ____________________________        8. ____________________________
                                       9. ____________________________
                                       10. ___________________________

Next-morning recall (no looking):  repetition ___/5    meaning ___/5
What I conclude: ____________________________________________________
```

## Template: 7-night sleep log

```
Night | In bed | Up    | Hours | Rested (1-5) | Screen in last hour? | Note
1     | ______ | _____ | _____ | ____         | yes / no             | ____
2     | ______ | _____ | _____ | ____         | yes / no             | ____
3     | ______ | _____ | _____ | ____         | yes / no             | ____
4     | ______ | _____ | _____ | ____         | yes / no             | ____
5     | ______ | _____ | _____ | ____         | yes / no             | ____
6     | ______ | _____ | _____ | ____         | yes / no             | ____
7     | ______ | _____ | _____ | ____         | yes / no             | ____
Average hours: ____   My one change for next week: ________________________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Learning facts by chanting them.** Repetition alone fades fast. Spend the same minute asking why, linking or picturing.
- **All-nighters before an exam.** You lose the sleep that consolidates what you studied. Stop new topics the evening before and sleep.
- **Believing you are too old to learn.** Adult brains keep changing with practice. Time and method matter more than age.
- **Treating sleep as wasted study time.** Sleep is when memories settle. Seven hours or more is part of the plan, not a break from it.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which way of learning "Article 17: abolition of untouchability" creates the strongest memory?
    - A) Highlighting it in yellow
    - B) Copying it five times
    - C) Repeating it twenty times
    - D) Linking it to the temple-entry movements and asking why it was needed
2. How much sleep does the AASM and Sleep Research Society consensus recommend for adults?
    - A) 7 hours or more a night, regularly
    - B) 4 hours plus naps
    - C) 5 hours if you study hard
    - D) 10 hours or more
3. What is consolidation?
    - A) The brain stabilising new memories over hours and during sleep
    - B) Joining a study group
    - C) Writing a summary
    - D) Reading a chapter twice
4. What did Dresler and others (2017) show about adults?
    - A) Only memory champions can use the memory palace
    - B) Adults cannot improve their memory
    - C) Brain training apps raise intelligence
    - D) Six weeks of memory-palace training improved memory and changed brain networks

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax 8.1 on encoding, 4.3 on sleep stages and the AASM sleep recommendation
- **Action:** Run the 10-fact encoding experiment and keep a 7-night sleep log. It is done when your proof is saved: your 10-fact experiment with both scores, and the 7-night sleep log with your one change.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Meaning-based (elaborative) encoding gives the fact many hooks in long-term memory.
2. **A.** Less than 7 hours regularly is linked with impaired performance and more errors.
3. **A.** New memories are fragile at first and are stabilised over time, with sleep playing a part.
4. **D.** It is good evidence of adult neuroplasticity; you build your own memory palace in Module 11.

sections.title: LRN-M01-L03: Retrieval and the forgetting curve
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain the forgetting curve and the testing effect, and prove to yourself with your own PSC facts that recalling beats rereading. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 30 minutes action over three days).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### The forgetting curve

In the 1880s Hermann Ebbinghaus learned lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself after different delays. He found that forgetting is fast at first and then slows down: much of what you learn today is gone within a day or two unless you do something about it. In 2015, Murre and Dros repeated his experiment carefully and got a very similar curve ([PLOS ONE, open access](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0120644)).

You have felt this curve. You read a chapter on the Kerala renaissance on Monday, understood it, and on Saturday you can name only two reformers. Nothing was wrong with your brain: that is how memory works.

### Retrieval changes the curve

**Retrieval** means pulling information out of memory: answering a question, writing what you remember on a blank page, explaining it aloud. Every time you retrieve something successfully, the memory becomes stronger and is forgotten more slowly next time.

The classic demonstration is by Roediger and Karpicke (2006). Students read short prose passages. Some reread them several times; others read once and then recalled them on blank paper several times. After 5 minutes, rereading did slightly better. After a week, the picture reversed: in one experiment, students who had studied once and recalled three times remembered 61% of the ideas, while those who had studied four times remembered 40% ([Roediger and Karpicke, PDF](https://psychology.ecu.edu/wp-content/pv-uploads/sites/216/2019/03/Roediger-Karpicke-2006.pdf)).

The same study found something important about feelings: the rereaders were **more confident** they had learned the material, although they remembered least. Rereading feels like learning because the page looks familiar. Recall feels harder, and that effort is exactly what makes it work.

### Desirable difficulty, with feedback

Effortful recall that mostly succeeds is ideal. Some struggle is good; complete failure is not. So:

- **Recall first, then check.** After recalling, open the book and fix what you missed or got wrong, preferably in a different colour so you can see your gaps.
- **Don't wait too long for the first review.** A first recall the same day or the next day catches facts before they fall off the curve.
- **Space the next reviews out:** 1 day, 3 days, 7 days and so on. Each review flattens the curve a little more. Module 3 turns this into a revision schedule, and Module 4 lets AnkiDroid do it for single facts.

### Forgetting is useful

Forgetting tells you what to review. A fact you recall easily needs less attention; a fact you keep forgetting needs a better hook (Module 3), a flashcard (Module 4) or a mnemonic (Module 11). Your weekly review (from this week) is where you look at what you forgot and decide what to do.

## Local example

**Anu** used to prepare a chapter by reading it twice in the evening with a highlighter, and she felt she knew it. A week later, in a practice test, she could not remember who founded the Sree Narayana Dharma Paripalana Yogam or when the Vaikom Satyagraha began, although she had highlighted both.

She ran the experiment in this lesson on the Kerala renaissance. She took 20 facts and split them into two sets of 10. Set A she read three times on Monday. Set B she read once, then wrote everything she could remember on a blank page, checked it, and did the same again 20 minutes later and once more on Tuesday.

On Thursday she tested both sets without looking. Set A: 4 out of 10. Set B: 8 out of 10. The extra time for set B was about ten minutes. She now ends every reading session by closing the book and writing for five minutes, and she says it feels harder, which is the point.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retrieval practice (the testing effect) | **Strong** | Rated high utility by Dunlosky and others (2013); shown in labs and classrooms, including Roediger and Karpicke (2006). |
| The forgetting curve: fast loss, then slower | **Strong** | Ebbinghaus's result was replicated by Murre and Dros (2015). |
| Spaced reviews slow forgetting | **Strong** | Distributed practice is rated high utility by Dunlosky and others (2013). |
| Rereading feels effective | **Strong** | It feels effective but isn't: rereaders were more confident and remembered less after a week (Roediger and Karpicke). |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Nicky Case, "How To Remember Anything Forever-ish" (interactive comic, public domain)](https://ncase.me/remember/) | Read the whole comic: the forgetting curve, the Leitner box and why spacing works | 25 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Roediger and Karpicke (2006), "Test-Enhanced Learning" (PDF)](https://psychology.ecu.edu/wp-content/pv-uploads/sites/216/2019/03/Roediger-Karpicke-2006.pdf) | Read the abstract and look at the results of Experiment 2 (repeated study versus repeated testing) | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Murre and Dros (2015), "Replication and Analysis of Ebbinghaus' Forgetting Curve", PLOS ONE](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0120644) | Read the abstract and look at the forgetting curve figure | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [The Learning Scientists: retrieval practice materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/retrieval-practice) | Download the retrieval practice poster and keep it on your phone | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Take 20 new facts from your current PSC topic (a chapter you haven't studied yet). Split them into set A and set B, 10 each, of similar difficulty.
2. Day 1, set A: read the 10 facts three times, carefully. No recall, no writing.
3. Day 1, set B: read the 10 facts once. Close the book and write everything you remember on a blank page. Check and correct in another colour. Twenty minutes later, recall them again on a fresh page and check.
4. Day 2: recall set B once more on a blank page and check. Don't look at set A.
5. Day 3 or 4: test both sets without looking, on a fresh page. Score each out of 10.
6. Write three lines: your two scores, how confident you felt about each set on day 1, and the study rule you will follow from now on.

**Proof to record:** Your recall pages for set B, the final test page with both scores, and your three lines.

## Template: recall versus reread experiment

```
RECALL vs REREAD      Topic: ______________   Start date: ______

SET A (reread 3 times on day 1)        SET B (read once, recall twice on day 1, once on day 2)
1. ________________________            1. ________________________
2. ________________________            2. ________________________
...                                     ...
10. _______________________            10. _______________________

Day 1 confidence (1-5): set A ___  set B ___
Final test on day ___ (no looking):  set A ___/10   set B ___/10
My rule from now on: _________________________________________________
```

## Template: blank-page recall routine (use after every reading session)

```
1. Close the book and turn the phone over. Timer: 5 minutes.
2. Write everything you remember: names, dates, causes, a diagram. No peeking.
3. Open the book. In a different colour, add what you missed and fix errors.
4. Circle the gaps. They are tomorrow's first recall.
5. Log it: Study Log -> Method = "retrieval", and what you recalled.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Rereading until the page feels familiar.** Familiar is not the same as remembered. Close the book and recall instead.
- **Recalling without checking.** Always check after recall, so errors are corrected instead of strengthened.
- **Waiting a week for the first review.** By then most of it is gone. Do the first recall the same day or the next day.
- **Judging methods by how they feel.** Effortful recall feels worse and works better. Judge by your test scores days later.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. In Roediger and Karpicke's experiment, which group remembered more after a week?
    - A) Both groups remembered the same
    - B) Students who read four times
    - C) Students who highlighted the passage
    - D) Students who read once and recalled three times
2. What is the shape of the forgetting curve?
    - A) No forgetting for a week, then sudden loss
    - B) Fast forgetting at first, then slower
    - C) Slow at first, then fast
    - D) A straight line down
3. Why do many students prefer rereading?
    - A) It uses more effort
    - B) It produces better results after a week
    - C) The page feels familiar, so they feel they have learned it
    - D) It is recommended by research
4. What should you do right after a blank-page recall?
    - A) Check against the book and fix gaps in another colour
    - B) Throw the page away
    - C) Move straight to a new chapter
    - D) Recall again immediately without checking

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Nicky Case's comic and the key results of Roediger and Karpicke (2006)
- **Action:** Run the recall-versus-reread experiment on 20 PSC facts and write your rule. It is done when your proof is saved: your recall pages for set B, the final test page with both scores, and your three lines.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** In Experiment 2, repeated testing gave 61% after a week and repeated studying 40%.
2. **B.** Ebbinghaus found it, and Murre and Dros (2015) replicated it.
3. **C.** Familiarity creates confidence without lasting memory.
4. **A.** Feedback corrects errors so you don't strengthen wrong answers.
